Welcome to Day 5 of health insurance subrogation training. Today we look at the health insurers you will meet most often, how reduction requests work, how subrogation applies to UM and UIM recoveries, and how PIP and health insurance interact. As a Closing Specialist, all of this feeds straight into the liens you resolve before a client is paid. Keep your questions coming as we go.

Here is our road map for today. First, the most common health insurances and how each handles subrogation. Second, reductions: when PIP can be waived and how to ask a lien holder to reduce. Third, UM and UIM subrogation. Fourth, how PIP insurance and health insurance work together. We finish with a summary. Each topic connects to the same goal: resolving every lien correctly before disbursement.

We start with TRICARE. It provides civilian health benefits for U.S. armed forces military personnel, military retirees and their dependents, and some reserve members. So when your client is in the military, retired from it, or is a family member of someone who is, expect TRICARE to be in the picture. Ask about military connections early so this lien does not surprise you at closing.

This slide describes TRICARE in a bit more detail. It is the healthcare program serving uniformed service members, retirees and their families worldwide, and it provides comprehensive coverage including medical, dental and pharmacy benefits. For our files, that means TRICARE may have paid for a wide range of accident-related treatment. When you review its payments, make sure every charge actually relates to the accident.

TRICARE comes in several plan options: TRICARE Prime, TRICARE Select, TRICARE Reserve Select and TRICARE For Life, each built for different beneficiaries. The program is managed by the Defense Health Agency under the Department of Defense. You do not need to memorize the plan names, but note which one appears on the client's card. If anything about TRICARE is unclear on a file, ask before you act.

Now TRICARE subrogation itself. After TRICARE covers the medical expenses, it seeks reimbursement from the third party responsible for the injury. The first two key points: TRICARE pays the medical bills first, and then it pursues reimbursement from the at-fault party or their insurance. In practice, that recovery comes out of our client's settlement, so the TRICARE claim has to be on our lien list. The other two key points. Beneficiaries must provide information and cooperate with TRICARE's efforts, and they must repay TRICARE from any settlement or judgment they receive. The slide closes with a reminder that beneficiaries need to follow TRICARE's subrogation rules to avoid complications. For us, that means responding to TRICARE requests promptly and getting its final amount in writing before any funds go to the client.

Practically, you usually will not deal with TRICARE directly on recovery. According to this slide, its subrogation efforts are handled by a dedicated contractor, referred to as the TRICARE Subrogation Contractor or TRICARE Recovery Audit Contractor. So when you open the claim, find out which contractor is handling it and send your correspondence there. Sending letters to the wrong office only delays the final lien amount.

This slide covers ERISA plans, which are employer-sponsored health plans. The tricky part is identifying them, because an ERISA member's card often looks just like an ordinary HMO card. That is why we request the plan documents. The US Airways v. McCutchen case is the reminder that the plan's terms matter, so we need to see them before assuming anything about the lien. Ask the group: what do we request when we suspect ERISA?

ERISA covers more than health insurance. There are health insurance plans with medical, dental and vision coverage from an employer; pension plans, such as 401(k) and defined benefit plans; and welfare benefit plans covering disability, life insurance and accident benefits. For our liens, the health plan is usually the one asserting reimbursement, but knowing the categories helps you understand what the client's employer actually provides.

Two regulatory points here. First, governance: ERISA sets standards for how these plans are administered, including fiduciary duties, reporting and disclosure, and participant rights. Second, preemption: ERISA preempts state laws on employee benefit plans, so federal rules generally override state regulations. That is why an ERISA lien can behave differently from other health liens, and why the attorney should review those files.

Let's return to the key point about ERISA plans before we move on. These are employer-sponsored health plans, and you usually cannot tell from the insurance card alone, because it looks like any standard HMO card. As the US Airways v. McCutchen case highlights, the safe practice is to request the plan documents so you know exactly which rules govern the subrogation claim.

Where does an ERISA plan's right to recover come from? Usually from a subrogation clause in the plan itself, allowing the plan to recover costs from the third party responsible for the injury. These clauses are usually set out in the Summary Plan Description, the SPD. That is the document to request and keep in the file whenever an ERISA plan asserts a lien.

Here is how an ERISA plan's subrogation process typically starts. First, claim identification: the plan spots potential subrogation cases when a claim is made for injuries caused by a third party. Second, notification: the plan notifies the responsible party or their insurer about its right to reimbursement. This is often why the plan or its vendor contacts us early, before the case has settled. The process continues with recovery: the plan seeks to recover what it paid on the beneficiary's behalf from the responsible party or their insurer. Then coordination: the plan works with other insurers where applicable and makes sure the beneficiary is not unjustly enriched. For you, this means confirming exactly which charges the plan paid, so nothing is counted twice across insurers.

The takeaway for ERISA is simple. For the specific subrogation provisions of any plan, go to the plan's SPD, or consult a benefits administrator or legal advisor. On our files, the legal advisor is the attorney. Do not guess at an ERISA plan's rights from memory or from another client's plan; each plan's own documents control.

Now a contrast. When the client buys their own health insurance rather than getting it through an employer, the insurer may not have a subrogation claim at all, so the client may owe nothing back. You will learn this when you open the health insurance claim. Even then, document it: note who confirmed there is no claim, so the file is clean at closing.

Now some of the large carriers. UnitedHealthcare typically handles subrogation internally. It investigates claims, seeks reimbursement from third parties, and coordinates with other insurers, and beneficiaries must cooperate by providing information and documents. When you open a UnitedHealthcare claim, confirm who in its recovery area is handling the file and keep every request and response in the file.

Cigna handles subrogation through its own department. It reviews claims, initiates subrogation proceedings against third parties, and works with other insurance providers, and beneficiaries need to cooperate and provide relevant details. The pattern is the same as the last slide: identify the contact, answer requests promptly, and get the lien amount confirmed in writing before closing.

Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield usually manages subrogation in-house. It identifies potential subrogation cases, pursues reimbursement from responsible parties, and coordinates with other insurers. Notice that beneficiaries are expected to give information and updates on settlements. So when an Anthem case settles, expect to report the settlement and request a final lien figure.

Humana also manages subrogation internally. It investigates to identify subrogation opportunities, pursues recovery from at-fault parties, and coordinates with other insurers, and beneficiaries must provide requested information and assist. As with the others, keep a record of every Humana request and our response, so the file shows we cooperated and the final figure is supported.

Kaiser Permanente handles subrogation internally as well. It identifies and pursues claims for reimbursement from third parties, and beneficiaries are required to cooperate and provide information related to the claim. Whichever carrier it is, your job is the same: find out who handles recovery, give them what they need, and confirm the final amount before disbursement.

Our last carrier is Aetna, which manages subrogation through its own department. It reviews claims, initiates subrogation actions, and works with other insurance companies, and beneficiaries should provide information and cooperate. Across all of these carriers, notice the common thread: each one expects cooperation, so prompt and documented communication protects our client and keeps closing on schedule.

Now we move to reductions, starting with PIP. According to this slide, when clients receive more treatment and follow-up recommendations, we can often get PIP completely waived. When a client has less treatment, the chances of a waiver drop significantly. So the treatment picture on the file matters when you ask. Check with your attorney on how this applies before making a waiver request.

A quick definition to anchor this section. Personal Injury Protection, or PIP, is auto insurance coverage that helps pay medical expenses and related costs after a car accident, regardless of who is at fault. Because PIP pays first and without regard to fault, the PIP carrier may later look to the settlement for repayment. That is why PIP shows up in our reduction work.

The slide says a Mahler reduction is typically the standard practice. If you believe a larger reduction is justified, you can ask for it, but be ready: the PIP adjuster will want specific details, including bills, third-party offers and other pertinent information. So gather that support before you send the request. A request without documents usually just comes back with questions.

Timing matters for a PIP waiver. PIP will only be waived once it is completely exhausted and the third-party limits are submitted. To start the waiver, send a request to the PIP adjuster. Generally, the adjuster will want the signed third-party release and the total billed amount. Have both ready when you send the request, so it is not delayed waiting on documents.

One more PIP point. When UM or UIM first-party limits are tendered, it usually results in an automatic PIP waiver. Usually is the key word. Never assume it: verify the waiver in writing and put that confirmation in the file. An unconfirmed waiver can turn into a PIP claim after the client has already been paid.

Now to subrogation lien reductions in general. Requesting a reduction means negotiating with the insurance company or lien holder to lower the amount they are seeking to recover. It is a negotiation, not a formality, so it needs a reason and support. Over the next slides we walk through the steps for doing it properly.

To request a reduction, the first step is identifying who actually holds the lien. It could be the client's health insurer, an auto insurer, or another party involved. Sending a reduction request to the wrong entity simply wastes time while the settlement sits. A common mistake is negotiating with one lien holder while a second is still unaddressed. How would you confirm you have found every lien holder?

Step two is reviewing the lien details. Gather every document related to the lien: the amount, the basis for the lien, and any correspondence from the lien holder. This is where you check that the charges relate to the accident and that the amount matches what was actually paid. You cannot argue for a reduction on a lien you have not read.

Step three is preparing the request. Draft a formal request that states the reason for the reduction, such as financial hardship or the portion of the settlement used for medical expenses, and attach supporting documents such as financial statements, medical bills and settlement details. A specific, documented request is far more persuasive than a one-line email asking for a discount.

Step four is submitting the request to the lien holder, by mail, email or their designated online portal. Follow any specific submission instructions the lien holder gives. If they require a portal or a particular form and you send something else, the request may never reach the right person. Note the date and method of submission in the file.

The final step is to document everything. Keep detailed records of every communication and document related to the reduction request. That trail matters if the lien holder later disputes the agreed amount, if another team member picks up the file, or if the attorney needs to see what was offered and accepted. If it is not in the file, it did not happen.

A reduction request leads to one of three outcomes. It may be approved, and you pay the lower amount. It may be rejected, and the request is denied. Or the insurer may counter with a different amount, often asking for settlement information first. Whatever happens, get the result in writing, and do not accept a counter offer without checking with the attorney.

Now UM and UIM. This slide addresses Medicare and Medicaid. The slide says subrogation does apply to them here, but it is essential that the client pays only their proportional share of the settlement if funds are limited. So when the recovery is small compared with the medical bills, raise the proportional-share question with the attorney before paying a government lien in full. This slide gives the case background. Referencing the Ahlborn case, it describes Farmers Insurance Exchange v. Forkey, where HHS sought full reimbursement for accident-related medical costs Medicare had conditionally paid. Medicare's claim to the uninsured motorist proceeds took priority over the widow's claim under Nevada's wrongful death law. The point for us: Medicare holds priority and has a stake in UM and UIM recoveries.

Now the general rules by plan type. For ERISA, subrogation reaches UIM if the plan expressly says so. For non-ERISA government plans in Nevada, NRS 689B.034(2) limits the right of lien or subrogation to a third person, though the government plan will argue that limit applies only to PEBP. These are legal judgments, so flag them for the attorney rather than deciding yourself. Two more categories. For non-ERISA plans in Nevada, the make whole doctrine and similar rules apply unless the plan language expressly excludes them, citing Canfora v. Coast Hotels and Casinos; the plan language decides UM and UIM applicability. For workers compensation, the 616.215 lien applies to the employer's UM or UIM only, not coverage paid for by employees. Always read the plan language.

Here is the basic UM and UIM subrogation process. After paying the client's medical expenses, the health insurer will assert a subrogation claim to recover those amounts from any available UM or UIM coverage. So a lien does not only attach to the at-fault driver's policy. A common mistake is assuming no lien applies because the money came from the client's own policy.

Two consequences for the client. First, the UM or UIM settlement might be used to reimburse health insurance before the client receives the remaining funds. Second, health insurance liens must be resolved before the final settlement is disbursed, according to the policy terms and legal requirements. For you, that means no disbursement until each health lien is confirmed in writing.

A short but important point. How health insurance subrogation is handled in UM and UIM cases can vary from state to state, including the rules on subrogation rights and lien recovery. The Nevada examples we just saw are one state's rules. Never carry a rule from one state's file to another; confirm with the attorney which state's law applies.

To wrap up UM and UIM: health insurance may seek reimbursement through subrogation for the medical expenses it paid. That means coordinating with the UM or UIM coverage, handling the legal and administrative side, and processing the client's settlement properly. Done well, the health insurance claim is addressed and the client's recovery is maximized. That is the balance we aim for on every file.

Our next section compares PIP and health insurance. Both cover medical expenses, but they do so in different ways and under different circumstances. On many of our files, the client has both, so you need to know which paid what and in what order. The next slides walk through how the two coverages interact and how reimbursement flows between them.

This is coordination of benefits. When both PIP and health insurance are available, PIP usually pays first, and after PIP is exhausted health insurance may cover the remaining costs. Coordination ensures neither policy pays more than the total medical expenses. Track exactly what each paid, so a bill is not counted twice. Why does the payment order matter when you review a lien ledger?

Sometimes the order is reversed and health insurance pays first. In that case, the health insurer may seek reimbursement from the PIP carrier. So the PIP carrier and the health insurer can end up settling accounts between themselves. Keep an eye on this when both are on a file, because it affects whose lien remains open at closing.

Because health insurance paid the medical expenses initially, it holds the lien against any settlement or recovery from the accident. That gives it the right to be reimbursed for what it paid. On your lien list, this is the entry you need confirmed. Make sure the amount reflects only accident-related payments.

Now, when PIP reimburses health insurance for those medical expenses, PIP essentially satisfies the health insurance lien. The PIP payment covers what the health insurer originally paid. For you, that means getting written confirmation from the health insurer that its lien is satisfied, so it is not paid a second time out of the client's settlement.

Here is that reimbursement process in two steps. First, the health insurer submits a claim to the PIP carrier for the medical expenses it covered. Second, the PIP carrier reviews the claim and, if approved, reimburses the health insurer. Until that payment is confirmed, treat the health insurance lien as still open on your closing documents.

The chain can go one step further. If the at-fault party's insurance agrees to the subrogation claim, the PIP carrier is reimbursed for the benefits it paid out, and that may involve negotiation over the amount. This happens between the carriers, but it can affect what the PIP carrier asks of our client, so keep track of it.

This flow shows how subrogation can chain when PIP is involved. The health insurer or its subrogation company may seek reimbursement from the PIP carrier, and the PIP carrier in turn may seek recovery from the at-fault party's insurance. Practically, you may see more than one party with an interest in the same medical payments. How many reimbursement claims could you be tracking?

A PIP subrogation lien is how a PIP carrier recovers what it paid for the insured's medical expenses and other losses from any settlement or recovery from the at-fault party. Managing it means coordinating with other insurers, negotiating, and complying with legal and regulatory requirements. Treat it like any other lien: identify it, confirm the amount, and resolve it before disbursement.

Let's summarize. Paying off subrogation liens means identifying and calculating every lien, negotiating reductions where needed, preparing and issuing payments, and keeping proper documentation and client communication throughout. Done carefully, every lien is resolved correctly and the client receives their settlement efficiently and without complications. The next few slides recap the key points of today's material.

First, understanding subrogation. It is the process by which a health insurer seeks reimbursement from another party, such as an at-fault driver's insurance, for the medical expenses it covered. The purpose is to recover costs the insurer paid because of an accident that is typically the responsibility of the at-fault party or their insurer. Everything else today builds on this definition.

Second, coordination with UM and UIM claims. Health insurance often acts as primary coverage for medical expenses, while UM or UIM can provide additional recovery when the at-fault party is uninsured or underinsured. And health insurers may assert subrogation rights against that UM or UIM coverage. So remember to check for a health lien on every UM or UIM recovery.

Third, the subrogation process. Health insurers submit a subrogation claim to the at-fault party's insurance or to UM or UIM coverage, detailing the medical expenses and payments made. Thorough documentation supports it: medical bills, payment records and evidence of coverage. When you review a lien, ask for these same records so you can check the amount claimed.

Fourth, paying off the liens. Identify them by gathering and reviewing all lien information from health insurance and every other insurer involved. Then calculate the total needed to satisfy all liens, issue payments to the lien holders, and confirm receipt. That last step is easy to forget. A payment is not finished until the lien holder confirms it was received.

Fifth, legal and administrative considerations. Be aware that state laws and regulations governing subrogation and lien recovery differ, and confirm the applicable rules with the attorney. Keep accurate records of all subrogation activity and make sure the file complies with legal requirements. Good records are what let anyone on the team pick up a file and see exactly where it stands.

Sixth, client communication. Keep clients informed about the status of their subrogation claims and how those claims affect their settlement. And support them after the settlement, addressing any remaining issues related to their recovery. Clients worry most when they do not know why their money is being held, so a short, clear update goes a long way.

Finally, complex cases. Make sure health insurance, UM or UIM coverage and other insurers are properly coordinated when a file has several of them. And when you face a complex subrogation issue or a dispute, seek legal advice; on our team, that means bringing it to the attorney. Escalating early is always better than guessing on a lien.

That completes Day 5 of health insurance subrogation training. We covered the common health insurers, reductions and PIP waivers, UM and UIM subrogation, and how PIP and health insurance interact. Take a moment to note one habit you will apply on your next file, and let's open the floor for any final questions.
